ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Comparing these classifications with the actual experimental conditions quantifies the kind of classifications that participants are asked to perform in typical awareness tasks, and provides the binary responses needed for any conventional SDT analysis.

> Figure 4 shows the estimates of the multilevel model for the two samples discussed in the section "Challenges for the Correlation and Intercept Hypotheses", in which each participant completed 80 (Panel A) or 20 (Panel B) trials per task.

> Under the model of Klauer et al. (1998), the multilevel SDT model accurately recovered both the population correlation and intercept, despite the violation of its assumed bivariate normal distribution, and even though up to 80% of participants had a true awareness-task sensitivity of exactly zero.

> In the subsequent conditioning test (influence task), CS-US pairings were randomized and conditioning was measured as 𝑑 ′ (e.g., a "pleasant" response counted as a hit when preceded by "NPLW" and as a false alarm when preceded by "DHJF", regardless of whether the word itself was pleasant or unpleasant).

> Eighty-six participants completed 360 trials per task, equally balanced between conditions.

> After the search task, participants completed an explicit recognition test (awareness task), identifying Old and New displays using a six-point confidence scale, allowing awareness to be assessed using both 𝑑 ′ and rating-based measures.

> Each participant completed 384 visual-search trials across 24 blocks (192 Old and 192 New), followed by 64 recognition trials (32 Old and 32 New), with responses ranging from 1 ("sure New") to 6 ("sure Old").

> To make this assumption more plausible,Reingold and Merikle (1988) recommended that the two tasks be as similar as possible, differing mainly in whether participants are explicitly asked to discriminate the relevant information.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

#### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository's files are grouped: the repository separates out studies (ex2b, ex3, ex4, ex5) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 41 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: open-document lock files (1), operating system (40). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 26272 columns across 1813 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1479 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1813 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Comparing these classifications with the actual experimental conditions quantifies the kind of classifications that participants are asked to perform in typical awareness tasks, and provides the binary responses needed for any conventional SDT analysis.

Figure 4 shows the estimates of the multilevel model for the two samples discussed in the section "Challenges for the Correlation and Intercept Hypotheses", in which each participant completed 80 (Panel A) or 20 (Panel B) trials per task.

Under the model of Klauer et al. (1998), the multilevel SDT model accurately recovered both the population correlation and intercept, despite the violation of its assumed bivariate normal distribution, and even though up to 80% of participants had a true awareness-task sensitivity of exactly zero.

In the subsequent conditioning test (influence task), CS-US pairings were randomized and conditioning was measured as 𝑑 ′ (e.g., a "pleasant" response counted as a hit when preceded by "NPLW" and as a false alarm when preceded by "DHJF", regardless of whether the word itself was pleasant or unpleasant).
Eighty-six participants completed 360 trials per task, equally balanced between conditions.

After the search task, participants completed an explicit recognition test (awareness task), identifying Old and New displays using a six-point confidence scale, allowing awareness to be assessed using both 𝑑 ′ and rating-based measures.

Each participant completed 384 visual-search trials across 24 blocks (192 Old and 192 New), followed by 64 recognition trials (32 Old and 32 New), with responses ranging from 1 ("sure New") to 6 ("sure Old").

To make this assumption more plausible,Reingold and Merikle (1988) recommended that the two tasks be as similar as possible, differing mainly in whether participants are explicitly asked to discriminate the relevant information.

Claims that the mind can process information without conscious awareness have broad implications for theories of perception, learning, and decision making.
However, commonly used statistical analyses can distort evidence, making unconscious processing appear stronger than it is.
Measures for these analyses often differ in scale and number of trials, making their sensitivities difficult to compare.
Moreover, analyses based on individual sensitivities often ignore measurement error, which can distort conclusions about unconscious processing.
We introduce a simple statistical framework that addresses these problems and allows researchers to evaluate three common hypotheses about unconscious processing within a single model.
We also provide free, open-source software to make this approach accessible to researchers.
Understanding cognition requires acknowledging that some cognitive processes operate outside conscious awareness (Hassin, 2013; Kihlstrom, 1987; Merikle et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Understanding cognition requires acknowledging that some cognitive processes operate outside conscious awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hassin, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kihlstrom, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Merikle et al., 2001</ref>).

text.text: Yet, demonstrating that a process is truly unconscious remains one of experimental psychology's greatest challenges (Holender, 1986; Newell & Shanks, 2014; Shanks et al., 2021; Stockart et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Yet, demonstrating that a process is truly unconscious remains one of experimental psychology's greatest challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Holender, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Newell & Shanks, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Shanks et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Stockart et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The difficulty is not simply to show that a stimulus or a regularity influences behavior, but to demonstrate that it does so in the absence of awareness.
Most research on unconscious processing can be broadly categorised into two types of paradigms.

In experiments on unconscious stimulus processing, researchers are often interested in testing whether individual stimuli (or a critical feature of it) can influence behavior without conscious awareness of those stimuli.

To this end, they often employ procedures that limit the conscious availability of the relevant information, such as masking or brief stimulus presentations, and examine whether this information can nevertheless influence performance (Kim & Blake, 2005; Kouider & Dehaene, 2007).
text.formatted: To this end, they often employ procedures that limit the conscious availability of the relevant information, such as masking or brief stimulus presentations, and examine whether this information can nevertheless influence performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Kim & Blake, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Kouider & Dehaene, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In other cases, stimuli are perfectly visible, but they are expected to influence behavior in ways that participants cannot detect or describe.

For instance, in experiments of implicit learning, researchers are typically interested in investigating whether learned regularities or stimulus contingencies acquired across many trials can influence behavior without conscious awareness of those regularities, although the stimuli are clearly visible (Frensch & Rünger, 2003; Perruchet & Pacton, 2006; Shanks, 2010).
text.formatted: For instance, in experiments of implicit learning, researchers are typically interested in investigating whether learned regularities or stimulus contingencies acquired across many trials can influence behavior without conscious awareness of those regularities, although the stimuli are clearly visible <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Frensch & Rünger, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Perruchet & Pacton, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Shanks, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, although these paradigms differ in the nature of the relevant information and how it is presented, both types of paradigms typically combine a measure of the influence of this information on behavior (hereon called "influence measure," but also known as indirect or implicit; Reingold & Merikle, 1988; Shanks & St. John, 1994) with a measure of awareness of such information (hereon called "awareness measure", but also known as direct 1 or explicit).
text.formatted: Thus, although these paradigms differ in the nature of the relevant information and how it is presented, both types of paradigms typically combine a measure of the influence of this information on behavior (hereon called "influence measure," but also known as indirect or implicit; <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Reingold & Merikle, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Shanks & St. John, 1994)</ref> with a measure of awareness of such information (hereon called "awareness measure", but also known as direct 1 or explicit).

text.text: Although the procedures used to measure influence and 1 Despite its popularity, we prefer to avoid the direct/indirect terminology, as it may be confusing for readers unfamiliar with it.
Although the terms "direct" and "indirect" refer to measures of processing, they can be misleading.
Using "direct measures of awareness" may wrongly suggest that awareness is measured directly, implying that the other also measures awareness, but indirectly.

Similarly, using "indirect measures of influence" may wrongly suggest that influence is measured indirectly, when in fact influence is measured directly (what is measured indirectly is awareness can vary considerably across studies (e.g., Stockart et al., 2025), claims of unconscious processing ultimately rely on establishing a dissociation between these two measures.

text.text: Much of the evidence for unconscious processing has been organized around three key hypotheses 2 (Shanks et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Much of the evidence for unconscious processing has been organized around three key hypotheses 2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Shanks et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The first, and perhaps the most common, is the group-level dissociation hypothesis, traditionally formulated as a simple dissociation: the relevant information influences behavior despite the absence of detectable awareness.

Conventionally, this hypothesis has been tested by conducting two separate tests at the group level, showing a statistically significant influence on behavior alongside a nonsignificant effect on awareness (Cheesman & Merikle, 1984).
text.formatted: Conventionally, this hypothesis has been tested by conducting two separate tests at the group level, showing a statistically significant influence on behavior alongside a nonsignificant effect on awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cheesman & Merikle, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: In a seminal study, for instance, Dehaene et al. (1998) found that masked number primes influenced responses to congruent targets by speeding them an average of 24 ms, although participants could not discriminate the primes significantly better than chance, concluding that semantic priming can operate in the absence of awareness.
text.formatted: In a seminal study, for instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Dehaene et al. (1998)</ref> found that masked number primes influenced responses to congruent targets by speeding them an average of 24 ms, although participants could not discriminate the primes significantly better than chance, concluding that semantic priming can operate in the absence of awareness.

text.text: Beyond this specific example, this kind of evidence has been used to claim unconscious processing in disparate literatures, such as reward-driven motivation (Pessiglione et al., 2007) or face perception (Finkbeiner & Palermo, 2009; Wójcik et al., 2019), as well as in lie detection (ten Brinke et al., 2014), response inhibition (van Gaal et al., 2010), fear conditioning (Öhman & Soares, 1998), relational memory (Reber et al., 2012), and visual statistical learning as measured by processes such as distractor suppression (Wang & Theeuwes, 2018) or contextual cuing (Chun & Jiang, 1998; Jiang et al., 2013), among others (Anderson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Beyond this specific example, this kind of evidence has been used to claim unconscious processing in disparate literatures, such as reward-driven motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Pessiglione et al., 2007)</ref> or face perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Finkbeiner & Palermo, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">Wójcik et al., 2019)</ref>, as well as in lie detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(ten Brinke et al., 2014)</ref>, response inhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">(van Gaal et al., 2010)</ref>, fear conditioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Öhman & Soares, 1998)</ref>, relational memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Reber et al., 2012)</ref>, and visual statistical learning as measured by processes such as distractor suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Wang & Theeuwes, 2018)</ref> or contextual cuing <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chun & Jiang, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Jiang et al., 2013)</ref>, among others <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anderson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The second is the correlation (or regression slope) hypothesis, which predicts that individual differences in the influence-task effect should not correlate with awareness across processing).

We do not consider this approach in the present article, because it has no straightforward solution from the model here presented-unlike the other hypotheses-, and because post hoc selection has been criticized not only methodologically (Rothkirch et al., 2022; Shanks, 2017; Yaron et al., 2024), but also conceptually (Schmidt et al., 2026).

Researchers test this hypothesis by computing, for each participant, a measure of influence (e.g., a difference score) and an awareness score, and then correlating these scores across participants.
A nonsignificant correlation is often taken as evidence that the measure of influence is driven by a process operating independently of awareness.

For example, Salvador et al. (2018) found that the effect of briefly flashed cues on memory suppression was unrelated to participants' ability to discriminate against those cues, even though discrimination was above chance at the group level, suggesting that memory suppression can be triggered by unconscious cues.

(2018)</ref> found that the effect of briefly flashed cues on memory suppression was unrelated to participants' ability to discriminate against those cues, even though discrimination was above chance at the group level, suggesting that memory suppression can be triggered by unconscious cues.

text.text: Similar null correlations have been taken as evidence of unconscious processing in literatures such as response inhibition (Chiu & Aron, 2014), syntactic priming (Berkovitch & Dehaene, 2019), affective priming (Wentura et al., 2025), contextual cuing (Colagiuri & Livesey, 2016; Geyer et al., 2010), working memory (Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026; Soto et al., 2011) statistical, sequence, and language learning (Batterink et al., 2015; Paciorek & Williams, 2015; Sanchez et al., 2010), and evaluative and classical conditioning (Dickinson & Brown, 2007; Jensen et al., 2015).

text.text: The third is the intercept hypothesis, which posits that the influence-task effect should be different from zero when awareness is assumed to be absent.
To test this hypothesis, researchers use the same participant-level scores as in the correlation hypothesis, but regress the influence-task effect on awareness (Greenwald et al., 1995).
text.formatted: To test this hypothesis, researchers use the same participant-level scores as in the correlation hypothesis, but regress the influence-task effect on awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Greenwald et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The intercept of this regression is the expected influence-task effect for a hypothetical participant with no awareness, so a significant intercept is typically interpreted as evidence that the effect persists in the absence of awareness. Berkovitch   and Dehaene (2019), for instance, concluded from a significant intercept that syntactic priming remained significant in participants with null sensitivity to the primes.

text.text: Taken at face value, these findings suggest that a wide range of cognitive processes can operate outside conscious awareness.

However, as several authors have pointed out, the methods traditionally used to test these hypotheses suffer from well-known problems that can systematically bias the evidence in favor of unconscious processing, casting doubt on the validity of such conclusions (Franco-Martínez et al., 2025; Klauer et al., 1998; Malejka et al., 2021; Meyen et al., 2022 Meyen et al., , 2024;; Miller, 2000; Newell & Shanks, 2014; Reingold & Merikle, 1988; Rothkirch et al., 2022; Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006; Shanks, 2017; Shanks et al., 2021; Shanks & St. John, 1994; Vadillo et al., 2016 Vadillo et al., , 2020 Vadillo et al., , 2022 Vadillo et al., , 2025)).

text.text: In the following sections, we first examine the methodological challenges of the conventional analyses to test the three hypotheses.
Next, we introduce a multilevel SDT model that addresses all these challenges within a single statistical framework.
Then, we present two simulation studies to review the performance of the multilevel SDT model.

Finally, we reanalyze three published studies on unconscious conditioning, contextual cuing, and masked affective priming using the open-source R package {uSDT} (Rey-Sáez, Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026), which we developed to make these analyses straightforward for applied researchers and which is publicly available on CRAN.
text.formatted: Finally, we reanalyze three published studies on unconscious conditioning, contextual cuing, and masked affective priming using the open-source R package {uSDT} (Rey-Sáez, <ref type="bibr">Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026)</ref>, which we developed to make these analyses straightforward for applied researchers and which is publicly available on CRAN.

text.text: When researchers attempt to establish a simple dissociation, that is, a significant effect in the influence task alongside with a nonsignificant effect in the awareness task, two methodological challenges arise.
First, inferring a null effect based on a nonsignificant result commits the well-known fallacy of accepting the null hypothesis (Dienes, 2014; Nickerson, 2000).
text.formatted: First, inferring a null effect based on a nonsignificant result commits the well-known fallacy of accepting the null hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dienes, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Nickerson, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As Carl Sagan (1977, p. 7) noted, "absence of evidence is not evidence of absence".
text.formatted: As Carl <ref type="bibr">Sagan (1977, p. 7</ref>) noted, "absence of evidence is not evidence of absence".

text.text: Thus, establishing a simple dissociation requires evidence that awareness is genuinely absent, not simply failing to detect that it is present.
Relatedly, the second challenge concerns statistical power.
The probability of detecting a true effect depends, among other factors, on sample size, the number of trials, and the amount of measurement error.
In practice, experiments on unconscious processing often collect substantially more trials in the influence task than in the awareness task.

Although in some studies awareness tasks may collect hundreds of trials (e.g., Greenwald et al., 1995; Greenwald & De Houwer, 2017), in most cases awareness is measured with only a few dozen (Vadillo et al., 2016) or even a single trial (Jiang et al., 2015; Wang & Theeuwes, 2018).
text.formatted: Although in some studies awareness tasks may collect hundreds of trials (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Greenwald et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Greenwald & De Houwer, 2017)</ref>, in most cases awareness is measured with only a few dozen <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">(Vadillo et al., 2016)</ref> or even a single trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Jiang et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wang & Theeuwes, 2018)</ref>.

Moreover, both influence and awareness measures often suffer from substantial measurement error, particularly when estimated from a limited number of trials (Hernández-Gutiérrez et al., 2025; Vadillo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, both influence and awareness measures often suffer from substantial measurement error, particularly when estimated from a limited number of trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Hernández-Gutiérrez et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Vadillo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This error further reduces the precision of the estimated effects and, consequently, the statistical power to detect them.
Combined with the differences in the number of trials, this may leave awareness tasks with considerably less statistical power than influence tasks.

This imbalance increases the probability of finding a significant influence effect alongside a nonsignificant awareness effect, even when participants have some conscious sensitivity to the relevant information.

Indeed, meta-analyses of hundreds of participants across studies have found above-chance awareness in paradigms where individual studies frequently failed to detect it (Hernández-Gutiérrez et al., 2025; Vadillo et al., 2016 Vadillo et al., , 2020)).

text.text: In other words, the traditional approach may produce apparent simple dissociations merely because awareness is often measured less precisely almost by design.

Regardless of these methodological challenges, what is perhaps less obvious is that this simple dissociation is often misinterpreted as evidence that the influence task is more sensitive to the relevant information than can be consciously reported in the awareness task (Meyen et al., 2022 (Meyen et al., , 2024)).

text.text: However, as Gelman and Stern (2006, p. 328) famously noted, "the difference between 'significant' and 'not significant' is not itself statistically significant".

text.text: Establishing that the influence task is more sensitive requires directly comparing the sensitivities of both tasks.

This alternative criterion, known as a sensitivity dissociationfoot_0 , has long been advocated as a way to move beyond the traditional requirement of demonstrating null awareness (Reingold & Merikle, 1988; Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006). 4Unfortunately, testing a sensitivity dissociation is not straightforward because influence and awareness effects are rarely measured in terms that allow to compare them in a common sensitivity metric (Meyen et al., 2022; Reingold & Merikle, 1988; Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006).

text.text: The problem is that these measures differ not only in their scales but also in what they quantify.
Sensitivity, as measured in typical awareness tasks, captures how well participants can use information available for explicit reporting to discriminate between experimental conditions.

Applying the same logic, a measure of sensitivity in RTs should discriminate between experimental conditions, so if we observed a RT from a single trial without knowing which condition produced it, how accurately could we identify that condition?
Consider two participants who achieve the same accuracy in an awareness task.
Participant 1 tends to respond "present" when the stimulus is actually present and "absent" when it is absent.
Participant 2, however, responds "present" much more often, even when no stimulus was shown.
If present trials are more frequent than absent trials, both participants can achieve the same accuracy, even though Participant 1 is better at distinguishing between the two conditions.
In other words, Participant 1's responses tell us more about whether the stimulus was actually present, and thus their awareness sensitivity is higher than that for Participant 2.
This is precisely what sensitivity 𝑑 ′ captures by taking both hits and false alarms into account.
The same might be applied to RTs.

Now, imagine two participants who show the same mean RT difference of 50 ms between experimental conditions (Figure 2). 5 For Participant 1, RTs are clearly different between conditions (due to small SD of 25 ms in each condition; Panel A), so knowing how long they took to respond would easily allow us to identify the condition.
text.formatted: Now, imagine two participants who show the same mean RT difference of 50 ms between experimental conditions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">5</ref> For Participant 1, RTs are clearly different between conditions (due to small SD of 25 ms in each condition; Panel A), so knowing how long they took to respond would easily allow us to identify the condition.

text.text: For Participant 2, however, RTs are much more similar across conditions (due to larger SD of 125 ms in each condition; Panel B), making it difficult to identify the condition from a single response.
This difference is reflected in their sensitivities.
Under the equal-variance SDT model, 𝑑 ′ can be expressed as the difference between conditions in units of the participant's own RT variability.
Thus, for Participant 1, a 50-ms difference corresponds to 2.00 SDs (50/25 = 2.00; Panel C), whereas for Participant 2 the same 50-ms difference corresponds to only 0.40 SD (50/125 = 0.40; Panel D).
In other words, Participant 1's RTs contain more information about which condition was presented, and thus their influence-task sensitivity is higher than that of Participant 2.
Moreover, even a measure with small sensitivity can produce a highly significant mean RT difference at the group level when enough trials are collected (Meyen et al., 2022).

text.text: Thus, comparing mean RT differences or accuracies is not equivalent to comparing sensitivities.
To establish that the influence task is more sensitive than the awareness task, both must be evaluated using a common sensitivity metric.

In fact, when findings traditionally interpreted as evidence of unconscious processing are reexamined using sensitivity comparisons, the evidence supporting these interpretations is often substantially weakened (Meyen et al., 2022 (Meyen et al., , 2024;; Schnepf et al., 2022; Zerweck et al., 2021).

text.text: The correlation and intercept hypotheses are also affected by measurement error, but with an important difference.

Whereas measurement error primarily reduces the precision of group-level estimates (affecting significance but not biasing the mean value), it can also systematically bias estimates of the relationships between tasks (i.e., correlation and regression parameters).
This problem arises from the two-step approach commonly used to test these hypotheses.
First, researchers compute a single score for each participant and task, such as a mean RT difference or a 𝑑 ′ .
Second, these scores are used in correlation or regression analyses, treating them as if they were measured without error.

However, as discussed above, participant-level scores estimated from a finite number of trials inevitably contain measurement errorfoot_3 , which can be substantial in experimental tasks (Enkavi et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; Yaron et al., 2024).

text.text: Note that these biases cannot be simply fixed by collecting larger sample sizes; with few trials, having more participants would only dangerously increase the confidence in biased estimations.
Finally, as illustrated above, the correlation hypothesis faces the same inferential challenge discussed earlier for simple dissociations.
A nonsignificant correlation does not establish the genuine absence of a relationship between influence and awareness.

Instead, researchers need methods that both address the impact of measurement error and can distinguish evidence for a null or negligible correlation from inconclusive results, such as Bayesian hypothesis testing (Dienes, 2014; Wagenmakers, 2007) or equivalence testing (Lakens, 2017).

As discussed in the Introduction, the group-level dissociation hypothesis concerns whether the influence task is more sensitive to the relevant information than the awareness task.

A meaningful comparison therefore requires two things: expressing sensitivity in both tasks on a common scale and collecting enough information from each task to achieve adequate statistical power to detect a difference between them.
We already explained why comparing the sensitivities of influence and awareness tasks requires both measures to be expressed on a common SDT scale (𝑑 ′ ).
When tasks involve binary discrimination responses-such as identifying whether a stimulus was present or absent-, sensitivity can be estimated directly from the trial-level responses using SDT.
However, when performance is measured using response times (RTs), an additional step is necessary because differences in mean RTs do not directly quantify sensitivity.
To overcome this challenge, we use the approach proposed by Meyen et al. (2022), which allows us to convert RTs into a measure of sensitivity similar to that of the awareness task.

For example, in a priming task where congruent trials are expected to produce faster responses, RTs below the median (i.e., fast responses) are classified as "congruent" and those above it (i.e., slow responses) as "incongruent".

Comparing these classifications with the actual experimental conditions quantifies the kind of classifications that participants are asked to perform in typical awareness tasks, and provides the binary responses needed for any conventional SDT analysis.
Under the appropriate assumptions, this procedure allows influence and awareness sensitivities to be estimated on the same scale.
Our multilevel model then jointly analyzes these trial-level classifications, estimating the sensitivities and their relationships.
Even when both tasks are expressed on the same sensitivity scale, individual sensitivity estimates remain subject to measurement error.
Imagine using a scale to compare the weights of two objects.
If each object is weighed only once, the observed difference may reflect their actual weights, random fluctuations in the measurements, or both.
By weighing each object repeatedly, we can see how much the readings vary even when the underlying weight remains unchanged.
The same principle applies to experimental tasks: observed differences between participants may reflect genuine differences in sensitivity, random variation across trials, or both.

By modeling individual trial responses, multilevel models can account for this latter source of variability when estimating individual sensitivities and how they vary across participants (Haines et al., 2025; Rouder & Haaf, 2019).

text.text: These five parameters contain all the information needed to evaluate our three hypotheses.

The group-level dissociation hypothesis concerns the difference in mean sensitivity between tasks (𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ), the correlation hypothesis concerns the association between true sensitivities (𝜌), and the intercept hypothesis concerns the expected influence sensitivity when awareness sensitivity is zero.
Under the assumed bivariate normal distribution, this last quantity corresponds to the regression intercept (𝛽 0 ) of true influence sensitivity on true awareness sensitivity:
By estimating these population parameters directly from trial-level responses, the multilevel SDT model allows researchers to evaluate all three hypotheses while accounting for measurement error.
It also accommodates differing numbers of trials across tasks and participants, and allows researchers to quantify the reliability of their measures.
In the next section, we introduce the multilevel SDT model used to estimate these parameters directly from trial-level responses.

Multilevel models (also known as hierarchical or mixed-effects models, Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002) are already familiar in experimental psychology, in part due to accessible tutorials and practical guidelines written for experimental psychologists (Baayen et al., 2008; Barr et al., 2013; Brysbaert & Debeer, 2025; Hoffman & Rovine, 2007; Meteyard & Davies, 2020; Singmann & Kellen, 2020).

text.text: Their main advantage is that they naturally accommodate the hierarchical structure of experimental data: trial responses (level 1) nested within participants (level 2).

Within this framework, trial-to-trial variability within participants (i.e., measurement error) is modeled separately from variability in participant-specific parameters (i.e., true individual differences).

In this sense, multilevel models can be conceptualized as psychometric models in experimental psychology, and have been used to estimate correlations corrected for measurement error across tasks (Rouder et al., 2023; Rouder & Haaf, 2019), as well as test-retest reliability (Haines et al., 2025; Rouder & Haaf, 2019).

text.text: Building on this foundation, we introduce a multilevel SDT model that jointly analyzes trial-level responses from the awareness and influence tasks.

We begin by assuming that both tasks are expressed on a common sensitivity scale, either directly or by applying the transformation proposed by Meyen et al. (2022) to the influence measure, where all responses, either discrete or continuous (such as RTs), will be transformed first into "classifications" following the standard logic of SDT.

text.text: Let 𝑦 𝑖 𝑗ℓ denote the observed response of participant 𝑖 in task 𝑗 on trial ℓ, coded as 1 for one response category and 0 for the other.

For example, in a typical priming experiment, participants' RTs may be used to classify trials as congruent (1) or incongruent (0), or displays as repeated (1) or new (0) in the case of a contextual cuing experiment, as we illustrate below.
We assume that each response follows a Bernoulli distribution: where 𝜋 𝑖 𝑗ℓ is the probability of a response coded as 1 on that trial.

This probability is modeled using a probit regression: where Φ -1 is the inverse standard normal cumulative distribution function (i.e., the "probit" link function), 𝑥 𝑖 𝑗ℓ represents the experimental condition (coded as 0.5 for signal trials and -0.5 for noise trials), and 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝑗 and 𝑐 𝑖 𝑗 are the participant-and task-specific sensitivity and response criterion, respectively.
We further assume that these participant-and task-specific parameters jointly follow a multivariate normal distribution: (
Here, 𝒅 ′ 𝑖 = (𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝐴 , 𝑑 ′ 𝑖𝐼 ) ⊤ contains participant 𝑖's sensitivities in the awareness (𝐴) and influence (𝐼) tasks, while 𝒄 𝑖 = (𝑐 𝑖 𝐴 , 𝑐 𝑖𝐼 ) ⊤ contains the corresponding response criteria.
The vectors 𝝁 𝑑 ′ and 𝝁 𝑐 contain the population means of these parameters, known as fixed effects in multilevel terminology.
Individual participants can deviate from these means, and these deviations are the random effects.
The matrix 𝚺 describes how much these random effects vary across participants and how they covary.
Its upper-left block, 𝚺 𝑑 ′ , contains the variances of true sensitivities and their covariance across tasks, while 𝚺 𝑐 describes the corresponding variances and covariance of response criteria.
Finally, the off-diagonal blocks, 𝚺 𝑑 ′ 𝑐 = 𝚺 ⊤ 𝑐𝑑 ′ , describe how sensitivities and response criteria covary, both within and across tasks.
Notice that 𝝁 𝑑 ′ and 𝚺 𝑑 ′ are exactly the mean vector and covariance matrix of true sensitivities introduced in Equation 1.
This means that the five population parameters defining our three hypotheses are estimated directly by the multilevel SDT model itself.

Because these parameters are estimated jointly from trial-level responses, the model accounts for measurement error without requiring separate estimates of individual sensitivities or their reliability.
All three hypotheses can therefore be tested using the model's parameters, avoiding the distortions introduced by the conventional two-step approach.
As shown in Equation 4, the participant-specific sensitivities, 𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝑗 , are themselves parameters of the multilevel model.

As discussed earlier, these parameters can be understood as true sensitivities, in the sense that they represent the values that would be recovered from infinite trials, assuming the model is correctly specified.
However, this does not mean that the model can recover these values perfectly from a finite number of trials.
Consider a participant whose observed sensitivity is unusually high after completing only a few trials, so this estimate is highly uncertain.

Multilevel models address this uncertainty by estimating individual sensitivities using both the participant's responses and the information shared with the rest of the group, represented by the multivariate normal distribution in Equation 5.

The resulting estimates represent a compromise between these two sources of information: the less reliable a participant's observed sensitivity, the more their estimated sensitivity is pulled toward the group mean.

To improve these predictions, partial pooling exploits the classical bias-variance tradeoff (Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017), introducing some bias toward the population mean in exchange for reduced estimation variance (Efron & Morris, 1975; James & Stein, 1961).

text.text: A perhaps surprising consequence is that, if we calculated the sample variance of these individual estimates, we would generally obtain a smaller value than the corresponding variance in Equation 5 estimated by the multilevel model (Louis, 1984; Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2004).

text.text: The same applies to covariances, which will generally differ from those estimated in 𝚺 𝑑 ′ .

Although both sets of quantities may appear to describe the same individual differences, the former describe the variability of individual predictions, whereas the latter describe the variability of true sensitivities in the population.
Correlations and regression coefficients calculated from these predictions can therefore yield biased estimates of population relationships (Devlieger et al., 2016; Skrondal & Laake, 2001).
text.formatted: Correlations and regression coefficients calculated from these predictions can therefore yield biased estimates of population relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Devlieger et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Skrondal & Laake, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: 9   For population-level inference, we should instead use the parameters estimated directly by the multilevel model.
The correlation between true sensitivities can be obtained from 𝚺 𝑑 ′ , while the regression intercept can be calculated from the population parameters, as shown in Equation 2.

Other individual-difference questions can often be addressed by extending the model to include additional covariates or outcomes, allowing the relationships of interest to be estimated while accounting for measurement error.
However, accounting for measurement error does not eliminate uncertainty when few trials are available.
Even when both tasks are expressed on a common sensitivity scale, differences in the number of trials can still affect statistical power.

As illustrated in Figure 5, collecting too few trials in one of the tasks can make genuine differences in sensitivity between tasks difficult to detect (and the multilevel SDT model cannot fix this, as we say in Spain: "Where there's no sprout, there's no spud.").
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>, collecting too few trials in one of the tasks can make genuine differences in sensitivity between tasks difficult to detect (and the multilevel SDT model cannot fix this, as we say in Spain: "Where there's no sprout, there's no spud.").

text.text: Thus, a meaningful sensitivity comparison requires not only comparable measures, but also sufficient information from both tasks.
To address this limitation, the {uSDT} package also allows researchers to evaluate statistical power when planning the sample and trial size of their experiments.

text.text: This extension is relatively straightforward and is already implemented in the {uSDT} package: the model structure remains unchanged, but prior distributions are assigned to its parameters.
Combining these priors with the observed trial-level likelihood yields posterior distributions for all model parameters, including the five population parameters defining our three hypotheses.

These posterior distributions can be used to compute credible intervals and, with appropriate prior specifications, Bayes factors to quantify evidence for or against the null hypotheses (Dienes, 2014; Wagenmakers, 2007).
text.formatted: These posterior distributions can be used to compute credible intervals and, with appropriate prior specifications, Bayes factors to quantify evidence for or against the null hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dienes, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Wagenmakers, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: One important consideration is that specifying priors on the five population parameters in Equation 1 also implicitly defines a prior on the regression intercept in Equation 2, since the intercept is a function of these parameters.
This induced prior may not reflect the researcher's prior expectations when testing the intercept hypothesis using Bayes factors.

When previous empirical evidence informs the priors on these population parameters, researchers can inspect the resulting prior on the intercept through prior predictive checking (Gelman et al., 2020) to assess its plausibility.
text.formatted: When previous empirical evidence informs the priors on these population parameters, researchers can inspect the resulting prior on the intercept through prior predictive checking <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gelman et al., 2020)</ref> to assess its plausibility.

text.text: Alternatively, the model can be parameterized as a latent regression (with the argument latent = "regression" in the hsdt() function), allowing a prior to be specified directly on its intercept.
In this parameterization, the intercept replaces the influence-task mean sensitivity (𝜇 𝐼 ), while the remaining four population parameters keep their own priors.
The influence-task mean is no longer sampled directly, but is derived at each posterior draw by solving Equation 2 for 𝜇 𝐼 .

As a result, both the intercept and the correlation between sensitivities (𝜌) have priors chosen by the researcher, whereas the prior on the group-level difference (𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ) is induced by the others.

The Bayesian framework also allows us to consider a more flexible version of the model that relaxes the equal-variance assumption of SDT (with the argument unequal_variances = TRUE in the hsdt() function).
The model presented in Equation 4 assumes that the underlying signal and noise distributions have the same variance.
Relaxing this assumption introduces an additional parameter that cannot be identified from binary responses without further assumptions.
However, Lages (2024) showed that this limitation can be overcome using a Bayesian hierarchical model that exploits variability in hit and false-alarm rates across participants.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Lages (2024)</ref> showed that this limitation can be overcome using a Bayesian hierarchical model that exploits variability in hit and false-alarm rates across participants.

text.text: Assuming that sensitivity and response criterion are independent at the population level (i.e., 𝚺 𝑑𝑐 = 0), and that the relative variances of the signal and noise distributions are approximately constant across participants, the ratio of the variances of their z-transformed false-alarm and hit rates can be used to estimate the relative variances of the underlying signal and noise distributions.
The multilevel SDT model makes several assumptions about how responses are generated and how sensitivities vary across participants.
At the trial level, it assumes normally distributed evidence with equal variances across stimulus conditions, although our Bayesian extension relaxes the equal-variance assumption.
It also requires that performance in both tasks can be expressed on a common sensitivity scale.
For tasks based on RTs, this involves converting continuous responses into binary outcomes, and the choice of conversion may affect the results.
At the participant level, sensitivities and response criteria are assumed to follow a single multivariate normal distribution.
This last assumption deserves particular attention.
A single normal distribution represents individual differences as continuous variation within one population.
However, some theories propose that aware and unaware participants constitute qualitatively distinct populations (Goldstein et al., 2022; Lublinsky et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, some theories propose that aware and unaware participants constitute qualitatively distinct populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Goldstein et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Lublinsky et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such an alternative could be accommodated within our framework using a mixture SDT model (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013), but would require additional assumptions about how these populations are defined.
text.formatted: Such an alternative could be accommodated within our framework using a mixture SDT model <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013)</ref>, but would require additional assumptions about how these populations are defined.

text.text: For example, should the unaware population include only participants with exactly zero awareness-task sensitivity, or also those with sensitivity below a specified threshold?
Furthermore, assigning participants to these populations would be uncertain when sensitivity is measured imperfectly.
Although mixture models can account for this uncertainty without requiring definitive classifications, they cannot determine what constitutes unawareness.
But suppose that aware and unaware participants do constitute distinct populations.
We would still be interested in the relationship between awareness and influence, particularly their correlation and regression intercept.

Can our multilevel SDT model accurately recover these parameters when the true population consists of distinct aware and unaware subpopulations, despite assuming a single multivariate normal distribution?
Simulation Study 2, presented in the next section, was specifically designed to address this question.
We conducted two simulation studies to evaluate the multilevel SDT model before applying it to empirical data.

Simulation Study 1 was a validation study in which data were generated from our model to assess parameter recovery and the validity of inferences on all three hypotheses across a broad range of conditions.

Simulation Study 2 was a robustness study examining whether inferences on the correlation and intercept remained valid when true sensitivities were generated from the alternative population models of Klauer et al. (1998) and Goldstein et al. (2022).
text.formatted: Simulation Study 2 was a robustness study examining whether inferences on the correlation and intercept remained valid when true sensitivities were generated from the alternative population models of <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Klauer et al. (1998)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Goldstein et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Both approaches were developed to estimate the relationship between awareness and influence measures while accounting for measurement error, but unlike our model both assume two subpopulations of participants: those with no awareness (𝑑 ′ 𝑖 𝐴 = 0) and those with positive awareness-task sensitivity.
Although they formalize these subpopulations differently, neither population model follows the bivariate normal distribution assumed by our model.
Here, we summarize the simulation designs and main results, with full methodological details provided in the Supplemental Material.

text.text: Inferences on H1 were valid at every level of reliability: the coverage of 𝜇 𝐼 -𝜇 𝐴 ranged from .917 to .970 and met Bradley's criterion in 99% of conditions.
For H2 and H3, results differed between low (𝑅 ≤ .3) and moderate to high reliability (𝑅 ≥ .4).
With 𝑅 ≤ .3, 48% of fits were untestable on average (up to 86%), leaving only a selected subset for inference.
In this subset, CIs for H2 were conservative in most conditions, but with 𝜌 = .8 their coverage fell below .925 in 68% of the conditions, down to .85.
Type I error for H2 was below .025 in 75% of null conditions.

Type I error for H3 met Bradley's criterion in only 46% of null conditions: it was conservative in 49% and exceeded .075 in 9 (maximum = .11), all with 𝑅 ≤ .2 and 𝜌 = .8, where the intercept was overestimated.
With 𝑅 ≥ .4, only 8% of fits were untestable, Type I error for H2 never exceeded .067, and Type I error for H3 met Bradley's criterion in 98% of null conditions (maximum = .073).
The power of H1 increased with effect size, sample size, and number of trials, as expected for a test of a group-level mean (Figure S6 in the Supplemental Material).

text.text: Goldstein et al. define the regression of influence-task sensitivity on awareness accuracy, rather than 𝑑 ′ .
This means that the regression is estimating an intercept closely related to that of Goldstein, but not exactly the same.
When awareness and the influence effect are related, our intercept is slightly larger than the one manipulated in their model, even when the latter is zero.

In our simulations, the difference was at most 0.045, and when the manipulated intercept was zero, H3 was rejected in up to 15% of the replications, with rejection rates above .075 in 13% of these conditions.
The difference comes from participants with almost perfect accuracy, which the model of Goldstein et al. allows.

text.text: If the accuracy of aware participants did not exceed .75 (i.e., a 𝑑 ′ of 1.35), the intercept defined by Goldstein et al. and the intercept estimated by our model would differ by at most 0.004.
The Supplemental Material reports these results in detail and explains where the difference comes from (Tables S10-S14 and Figures S9-S11).

text.text: Across experiments, participants categorized either words as "pleasant" or "unpleasant", or first names as "male" or "female".

During acquisition, each word or name (unconditioned stimulus, US) was preceded by one of two four-consonant strings (CSs; e.g., "NPLW" or "DHJF"), each consistently paired with one US category (e.g., "NPLW" with pleasant words and "DHJF" with unpleasant words).

In the subsequent conditioning test (influence task), CS-US pairings were randomized and conditioning was measured as 𝑑 ′ (e.g., a "pleasant" response counted as a hit when preceded by "NPLW" and as a false alarm when preceded by "DHJF", regardless of whether the word itself was pleasant or unpleasant).

In the masked-CS experiments, a subsequent visibility test (awareness task) required participants to identify which of the two consonant strings had appeared on each trial, measuring awareness with 𝑑 ′ as well.

Research on unconscious processing has traditionally relied on three types of evidence: group-level dissociations between influence and awareness measures, their correlation across individuals, and the intercept of their regression.

These hypotheses are often tested using separate analyses that overlook methodological challenges: differences in statistical power and measurement scales, measurement error, and the failure to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence.
Together, these challenges can artificially inflate the apparent evidence for unconscious processing.

Although several methods have been proposed to address each of these challenges in isolation, researchers must identify, understand, and implement the appropriate methods for each challenge, which can be highly demanding.
In this work, we have introduced a multilevel SDT model that simultaneously addresses these challenges and allows all three hypotheses to be tested in a single step, using just one R function.

By jointly analyzing trial-level responses from influence and awareness tasks, the model accounts for uncertainty in individual sensitivities and estimates the population parameters needed to evaluate each hypothesis.
To facilitate its use in applied research, we have implemented the models in the R package {uSDT}, available on CRAN (Rey-Sáez, Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To facilitate its use in applied research, we have implemented the models in the R package {uSDT}, available on CRAN (Rey-Sáez, <ref type="bibr">Garre-Frutos, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The package provides both frequentist and Bayesian implementations, allowing researchers to fit these models with minimal effort.
Although multilevel models account for measurement error, they cannot compensate for too low reliability.

When one or both tasks are highly unreliable (e.g., reliabilities below .30), the data may simply contain too little information to estimate the relationship between true sensitivities with sufficient precision.
This problem cannot be solved by statistical modeling alone, but the multilevel SDT model can at least alert researchers to the substantial uncertainty surrounding these estimates.

Nevertheless, researchers should prioritize improving task reliability through experimental design, for example, by increasing the number of trials or optimizing task procedures to obtain more precise measures of individual differences (e.g., Siegelman et al., 2017; Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026; Vadillo et al., 2025; Whitehead et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, researchers should prioritize improving task reliability through experimental design, for example, by increasing the number of trials or optimizing task procedures to obtain more precise measures of individual differences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Siegelman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Vadillo et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Whitehead et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Reliability alone, however, does not guarantee that our inferences are valid.

For instance, even when measurement error is minimized and a proper sensitivity comparison is computed, inferences about unconscious processing still depend on whether the awareness task adequately measures conscious awareness (e.g., Giménez-Fernández et al., 2020; Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026; Franco-Martínez, Ferrer-Mendieta, et al., 2026; Schmidt & Biafora, 2024).
text.formatted: For instance, even when measurement error is minimized and a proper sensitivity comparison is computed, inferences about unconscious processing still depend on whether the awareness task adequately measures conscious awareness (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Giménez-Fernández et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Franco-Martínez, Rey-Sáez, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Franco-Martínez, Ferrer-Mendieta, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Schmidt & Biafora, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond measurement validity, our model does not currently accommodate alternative criteria for inferring unconscious processing, such as the double-dissociation criterion proposed by Schmidt and Vorberg (2006).
text.formatted: Beyond measurement validity, our model does not currently accommodate alternative criteria for inferring unconscious processing, such as the double-dissociation criterion proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Schmidt and Vorberg (2006)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, note that the proposed framework could be readily extended to test this criterion with an appropriate experimental design, simply by framing H1 to test for an interaction.

But in any case, while statistical modeling can help to mitigate methodological issues and improve inferences in unconscious processing research, these models cannot, by themselves, ensure the validity of the measures on which those inferences rely.
Relatedly, another consideration concerns how influence and awareness are assessed.
Consider, for example, a masked priming experiment in which participants respond to targets preceded by briefly presented primes.

The influence of the primes can be assessed through their effects on RTs, whereas awareness can be measured either on the very same trials, by asking participants to report how clearly they perceived each prime (online), or in a separate detection or discrimination task (ofline, see Jimenez et al., 2025).

text.text: Like other approaches that estimate the relationship between influence and awareness across participants (Klauer et al., 1998; Goldstein et al., 2022.), our model does not explicitly account for these dependencies.

text.text: Whether and to what extent ignoring these dependencies affects the inferences drawn from such models remains to be assessed properly by future research.
A further limitation concerns the generalizability of correlations between influence and awareness tasks.
These correlations are inherently task-specific and cannot be directly interpreted as correlations between influence and awareness constructs.
This has been referred to as "task impurity" (Miyake et al., 2000), that is, no task can be a perfectly pure measure of a latent construct.
text.formatted: This has been referred to as "task impurity" <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Miyake et al., 2000)</ref>, that is, no task can be a perfectly pure measure of a latent construct.

text.text: With only one influence and one awareness task, we cannot aim to determine whether their relationship might generalize across different measures of the same construct.

A promising alternative is to collect multiple awareness and influence measures and analyze them using generalized hierarchical factor models (Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026; Rouder & Mehrvarz, 2026; Stevenson, Heathcote, et al., 2024; Stevenson, Innes, et al., 2024; Stevenson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A promising alternative is to collect multiple awareness and influence measures and analyze them using generalized hierarchical factor models <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Rouder & Mehrvarz, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stevenson, Heathcote, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Stevenson, Innes, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Stevenson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These models adapt exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis to experimental settings, allowing researchers to model awareness and influence as latent factors underlying their respective measures and estimate the correlation between them.

Their main advantage is that they do so by modeling trial-level responses within a hierarchical framework, as in our multilevel SDT model, but allowing for task-specific likelihoods (e.g., Bernoulli for binary responses or ex-Gaussian for response times).

Moreover, combining multiple tasks can improve the precision of estimates of true correlations between task effects by leveraging the information each task shares with the others (Mehrvarz & Rouder, 2025; Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, combining multiple tasks can improve the precision of estimates of true correlations between task effects by leveraging the information each task shares with the others <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Mehrvarz & Rouder, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Rey-Sáez, Franco-Martínez, Revuelta, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This approach would allow researchers to move beyond task-specific associations and examine whether awareness and influence performance share common underlying processes across different paradigms.
Claims that information can be processed without conscious awareness have important implications for theories of human cognition.
Yet such claims have often relied on inconsistent statistical evidence, small samples, few awareness trials, unreliable measures, and tests not suitable for evidence of absence.

Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence (Sagan, 1979), and we have shown that nonsignificant awareness effects, weak correlations, and significant regression intercepts can have much more ordinary methodological explanations, such as insufficient statistical power, differences in measurement scales, and measurement error.
text.formatted: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Sagan, 1979)</ref>, and we have shown that nonsignificant awareness effects, weak correlations, and significant regression intercepts can have much more ordinary methodological explanations, such as insufficient statistical power, differences in measurement scales, and measurement error.

text.text: Clearly, the multilevel SDT model (like any statistical model) cannot compensate for insufficient data or invalid measures, but it provides a robust model-based approach to assessing the strength of evidence for and against unconscious processing while accounting for measurement error and differences in scale.

We hope this framework, and its accessible implementation in the {uSDT} package, will encourage researchers to revisit established findings and design more informative studies capable of providing the robust evidence that claims of unconscious processing require.

In contextual-cuing paradigms, participants search for a target (a rotated T) among distractors (L-shaped), with some displays repeated across blocks (Old) and others presented for the first time (New).
Contextual cuing was measured as the difference in RTs between Old and New displays (influence task), with faster responses to Old displays indicating learning.

After the search task, participants completed an explicit recognition test (awareness task), identifying Old and New displays using a six-point confidence scale, allowing awareness to be assessed using both 𝑑 ′ and rating-based measures.
For our illustration, we use Experiment 2 with a Spanish sample (𝑁 = 104), which included a relatively large number of trials for contextual-cuing research.

Each participant completed 384 visual-search trials across 24 blocks (192 Old and 192 New), followed by 64 recognition trials (32 Old and 32 New), with responses ranging from 1 ("sure New") to 6 ("sure Old").

text.text: library(uSDT) # Trial-level data of both tasks, one row per trial # Awareness measure # Influence measure data(vadillo_awareness) data(vadillo_cuing) #> subj condition judged.old #> subj condition rt #> 1 2001 old 0 #> 1 2001 new 1305.352 #> 2 2001 old 1 #> 2 2001 old 4027.887 #> 3 2001 new 1 #> 3 2001 old 2484.210 # Both tasks in one object, with Old displays as signal trials d <-usdt_data_tasks( awareness = vadillo_awareness, influence = vadillo_cuing, subject_col = "subj", condition_col = "condition", condition_levels = c(signal = "old", noise = "new"), response_col = list(awareness = "judged.old", influence = "rt"), response_levels = list(awareness = c(signal = 1, noise = 0), influence = c(signal = "faster", noise = "slower")), dichotomize = list(awareness = FALSE, influence = TRUE)) # Fit the frequentist hierarchical SDT model and check results fit <-hsdt(d); summary(fit) # Other utilities usdt_reliability(fit) # Reliability estimates per task and participant plot(fit, type = "roc") # Our figure 8 in main text plot(fit, type = "regression") # Our figures 9 and 10 in main text # Bayesian model: set prior distributions (if not, default priors used) priors <-usdt_priors(intercept = "normal(0, 1)", cor_dprime = "lkj(1)") # Fit the Bayesian hierarchical SDT model and check results fit_b <-hsdt(d, estimation = "bayesian", priors = priors, latent = "regression") summary(fit_b) # Bayes factors and plots for the same hypotheses as the frequentist model usdt_bf(fit_b) # Bayes factors and plot type as in Figure 11 usdt_bf(fit_b, hypothesis = c("rho = 0", "rho > 0"))

We use the term group-level dissociation hypothesis to refer collectively to simple and sensitivity dissociations, which represent two distinct criteria for establishing a dissociation between influence and awareness(Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006).

text.text: However, greater sensitivity in the influence task does not, by itself, establish unconscious processing.
text.formatted: However, greater sensitivity in the influence task does not, by itself, establish unconscious processing.

text.text: This interpretation relies on the assumption that the awareness task is at least as sensitive to consciously available information as the influence task.
If this assumption holds, any additional sensitivity in the influence task cannot be explained by conscious information alone.

To make this assumption more plausible,Reingold and Merikle (1988) recommended that the two tasks be as similar as possible, differing mainly in whether participants are explicitly asked to discriminate the relevant information.
